f0.government: Frontier union of trading posts and settler councils
f0.summary: Fur traders, loggers and settler councils holding the vast northwest from the Pacific ports to the Arctic shore.
history: The Northern Union began as a compact between the fur companies of the Pacific coast and the settler councils of the interior, signed at Seattle in 1771 to keep the peace along the trade roads. Its councils never ruled much, but they ruled far: every post from the Alaskan ports to the shores of Baker Lake owes the Union its roads, its garrisons and its tariffs.

The Union's strength is distance. Its rivals would have to march for months through forest and tundra to reach anything that matters, and its trappers and rangers know every trail. Its weakness is the same: the Union is thinly settled, its harvests are short, and its armies are small for the ground they must hold.

The First Warden, Elias Marrow, is a former quartermaster who distrusts the Atlantic League's ambitions in the east and the southern nations' growing fleets. He keeps a fleet at Anchorage and the continent's only air group at readiness, and he means to use them.

traits.name: Trailwise
traits.effect: Land units pay 15% less movement in forests.

f1.summary: The chartered cities of the Atlantic seaboard and the Great Lakes, rich in trade and drilled regiments, hungry for the interior.
history: When the eastern colonies broke from their distant crown in 1776, the victors did not form one republic but a league: Boston, Toronto and a dozen lesser cities, each with its own charter, bound by a common treasury and a common army. The League's Chancellor is elected by the city councils and answers to the merchants who fund them.

The League is the richest nation on the continent and its regiments are the best drilled. Its merchant houses trade with every port from Havana to the Pacific, and its gold buys what its farms cannot grow. Its borders, though, are long, and it has quarrelled with the Northern Union over the lakes and with the Sierra Compact over the western trails.

Chancellor Ashdown won office promising to open the continent's interior to League settlers. Salt Lake City, founded by League companies beyond the plains, is the first fruit of that promise, and the one most exposed to attack.

f2.government: Compact of ranching provinces and frontier towns
f2.summary: Ranchers, riders and river towns of the southern plains and northern Mexico, united by the need to guard a long, open frontier.
history: The Sierra Compact was sworn at Ciudad Juárez in 1783 by the ranching families of the northern provinces and the new towns of the Texas plains, who had learned that no single one of them could hold the open country alone. Its Governor-General commands the Compact's riders; its provincial juntas levy their pay.

The Compact's lands are wide, dry and hard to defend, and its people have made a virtue of it. Its cavalry is cheap to raise from the ranches and fast on the open plains, and its towns of Houston and Fort Worth trade cattle and cotton down the rivers to the Gulf.

Governor-General Villarreal fought the Atlantic League's settlers on the northern trails as a young officer. He trusts horses more than walls and allies more than either, and he watches the Caribbean Accord's hold on Mexico City with open resentment.

f3.government: Maritime republic of island and coastal cities
f3.summary: A maritime republic joining the islands and coasts of the Caribbean, from Havana to Mexico City and Medellín, bound by its fleets.
history: The Caribbean Accord was born at sea. In 1790 the port cities of the islands and the Gulf coast, tired of paying tribute to distant powers, pooled their privateers into one navy and declared a republic with its capital at Havana. Mexico City joined for protection; Medellín for trade.

No nation on the continent builds ships more cheaply or sails them better. The Accord's harbours ship timber and sugar to every coast, and its merchants are as welcome in League ports as its warships are feared. On land it is weaker: its provinces are scattered across the sea and hard to supply.

Admiral-President Carranza commanded the fleet that won the Accord its independence. She believes the nation that rules the Caribbean Sea will in the end rule the continent, and she is building ships to prove it.

f4.government: Pact of highland provinces under an elected Protector
f4.summary: The highland provinces of the northern Andes and the Orinoco, a mountain fortress rich in silver and iron.
history: The Andean Pact grew out of the highland revolts of 1781, when the mountain provinces from Bogotá to Lima threw out their colonial governors and chose a Protector to lead their common defence. The Protector is elected for life by the provincial assemblies and may not raise taxes without them.

The Pact sits on the continent's great mountain wall. Its passes are few and easily held, its mines yield iron and silver, and its highland regiments have never lost a battle fought uphill. Beyond the mountains, though, its lowland provinces on the Orinoco and the coast are open to any invader.

Protector Quispe is a mining engineer turned soldier who built the Pact's foundries. He wants the Pact's lowlands secure before any rival can reach them, and he eyes the Amazon Federation's rivers as the road to doing it.

f5.government: Federation of river provinces and highland towns
f5.summary: A federation of the great river basins and the Bolivian highlands, feeding itself from rich harvests and moving along its rivers.
history: The Amazon Federation was formed in 1788 when the river towns of the interior, from Porto Velho to Goiânia, joined the highland city of La Paz in a federation to control the trade that flows down the great rivers. Its Speaker presides over a congress of river provinces that rarely agree on anything but defence.

The Federation's lands are the most fertile on the continent, and its river pilots move troops through forest that would stop any other army. It is, though, surrounded: the Andean Pact to the north and west, the Southern Coalition to the south, and the League's merchants eager for its harvests.

First Speaker Andrade came to office after a famine year, promising that the Federation would never again sell its grain while its own people went hungry. She wants secure borders and full granaries, and fears the Andean Pact's ambitions most of all.

traits.name: River Pilots
traits.effect: Land units pay 20% less movement in forests.

f6.government: Coalition of Chilean and Pampean provinces under a Director
f6.motto: From the mountains to the plains
f6.summary: A coalition across the southern Andes, joining the Chilean valleys to the pampas, famous for its horsemen.
history: The Southern Coalition joined the Chilean valleys and the cattle provinces of the pampas in 1785, after the two had fought each other to exhaustion over the mountain passes. Its Director governs from Santiago with a council of provincial governors, and its army is raised mostly from the estancias.

The Coalition's gauchos are the finest light horsemen on the continent, cheap to raise and at home on the open plains. Its lands are compact and well connected, but squeezed between the Amazon Federation to the north and the Austral Republic to the south, with little room to grow.

Director Echeverría is a cattle baron who won his office by ending the pass wars. He is cautious by nature, preferring alliances to battles, but he will not let the Austral Republic take the southern plains.

traits.name: Open Plains
traits.effect: Land units pay 10% less movement on plains.

f7.government: Republic of southern settlements under two Consuls
f7.summary: The hardy republic of Patagonia and the southern islands, provisioned for long winters and stubborn in defence.
history: The Austral Republic began as an expedition. In 1792 a company of settlers, whalers and soldiers founded Bahía Blanca at the edge of the southern plains and declared a republic, electing two Consuls in the Roman manner. Comodoro Rivadavia and the island settlement of Fox Bay followed.

The Republic's lands are cold, windy and far from everyone. Its settlers learned to keep great storehouses against the winters, and its militia to hold its forts against raiders from every direction. It is the smallest of the eight nations in people, but the hardest to dislodge.

Consul Montero, the senior of the two, is a former expedition captain with an eye on the rich plains to the north. His colleague counsels patience; Montero believes the Republic must grow or be swallowed.

traits.name: Expedition Stores
traits.effect: Stockpiles hold 50 more of each resource.

traits.name: Stubborn Defence
traits.effect: Units defend 10% better in the Republic's own provinces.
